title: The Old Guard
author: Debra Ducane

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Partial woke trap. The Netflix marketing for The Old Guard emphasized the action, Charlize Theron's warrior character, and the immortality premise. The significant LGBTQ content (Joe and Nicky as a centuries-long gay couple, including a passionate kiss and a monologue about romantic love between men) was not prominent in promotional materials. Conservative audiences who chose this based on the action premise could reasonably have been surprised by the prominence of the gay relationship. The anti-Big Pharma villain is also more politically explicit than the trailer suggests. That said, the film's traditional elements (sacrifice, duty, warrior brotherhood) are genuine and substantial enough that the TRADITIONAL LEAN verdict holds.

externalScores.netflixViews: 78M households in first 4 weeks (Netflix record at time of release)

director.name: Gina Prince-Bythewood
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT. Prince-Bythewood is a Black woman director known for Love & Basketball (2000) and Beyond the Lights (2014). She is a skilled filmmaker who works in multiple genres and brings emotional authenticity to action. She is progressive in her commitment to diverse representation but does not make ideological films in the sense of prioritizing message over craft. The Old Guard is her most action-heavy film and demonstrates genuine command of large-scale action sequences.
director.profile: Gina Prince-Bythewood's filmography shows consistent craft and emotional intelligence across genres. She approached The Old Guard as an action film that takes its characters seriously: the immortal warriors are not defined by their powers but by what those powers have cost them over centuries. Her direction brings weight and consequence to action sequences that could easily have been weightless. She subsequently directed The Woman King (2022), which received more polarized political reception. The Old Guard represents her work at its most accessible to mixed audiences.

writers.names: Greg Rucka (screenplay and source graphic novel)
writers.profile: Greg Rucka adapted his own graphic novel, published by Image Comics in 2017. Rucka is a prominent comics writer known for characters including Batwoman (who is lesbian), Renee Montoya, and others in the DC universe. His work consistently features LGBTQ characters in central roles. Joe and Nicky's relationship is a direct transfer from the source material. Rucka's screenplay is tighter than most superhero adaptations: the immortality mechanics are internally consistent, the villain's motivation connects to the heroes' purpose, and the emotional beats earn their weight.

lead_producer.name: David Ellison, Dana Goldberg, Don Granger, Marc Evans

composer.name: Volker Bertelmann (Hauschka)
composer.profile: Volker Bertelmann's score uses electronics and percussion to create a modern, kinetic sound that suits the film's contemporary setting and ancient backstory. The score does not try to sound 'epic' in the traditional superhero sense; it is grittier and more atmospheric, fitting for a film about immortal mercenaries who work outside official channels.

production_designer.name: Stephanie Collie
production_designer.profile: The production spans multiple locations: Morocco, Afghanistan, South Sudan, London, France. The design work is location-heavy rather than set-heavy, giving the film a naturalistic feel unusual for the action genre. The contrast between the ancient and modern in the characters' lives is reflected in the locations: the team operates in contemporary conflict zones while carrying memories of medieval battlefields.

fidelityCasting.assessment: The film is a faithful adaptation of Greg Rucka and Leandro Fernandez's graphic novel. Charlize Theron's Andy is faithful to the source's portrayal: ancient, tired, morally complex. KiKi Layne as Nile Freeman is consistent with the source's characterization of the newest immortal as a Black female Marine. Joe and Nicky's relationship is directly transferred from the graphic novel, including their status as a long-term gay couple. Matthias Schoenaerts as Booker is well-cast for the character's French and Napoleonic-era backstory. Chiwetel Ejiofor as Copley adds a Black actor to a character who is not specifically racialized in the source material. Harry Melling's Merrick is slightly more cartoonish than the source. Overall: a respectful and largely faithful adaptation.

parentalGuidance.mpaaDescriptors: Sequences of graphic violence, and language
contentWarnings: Frequent graphic violence: gunshot wounds, stabbings, and brutal combat throughout
The immortality conceit means characters are repeatedly killed and resurrected on screen, sometimes graphically
A character is shown repeatedly drowning and recovering over centuries, depicted with genuine horror
Joe and Nicky share a passionate kiss and an extended monologue about romantic love between men
A villain experiments on captive humans
No sexual content beyond the kiss mentioned above
Thematic content: questions about the meaning of immortal existence, the weight of centuries of violence, and whether life has purpose
parentalGuidance.guidance: Rated R. Appropriate for ages 16 and up. The violence is the film's primary content concern: it is frequent, realistic, and occasionally graphic. The immortality premise means characters die on screen multiple times, which young teenagers may find disturbing. The LGBTQ content (Joe and Nicky's relationship) is present and includes a kiss and an emotional monologue; families who prefer to avoid this content should know it is a meaningful element of the film, not a background detail. The thematic depth (what does centuries of existence cost a person? is there meaning in suffering?) is more appropriate for older teenagers and adults.

summary.overall:
The Old Guard surprised a lot of people when it became one of Netflix's biggest hits of 2020. The premise sounds like a standard action thriller: a team of immortal mercenaries, led by Charlize Theron's ancient Scythian warrior Andy, discovers they can die, while a newly immortal Marine named Nile threatens to expose their existence to a pharmaceutical executive who wants to exploit their regenerative abilities. What makes the film more interesting than that synopsis suggests is what the immortality actually means to the people who have it.

Andy (Andromache of Scythia) has been alive for roughly three thousand years. She has fought in nearly every major conflict in human history. She is exhausted in a way that no amount of sleep can fix. The film's opening image is her staring at the ceiling at 2am, unable to sleep, in the flat affect of someone who has done everything and found it insufficient. Charlize Theron plays this with her characteristic physical commitment and emotional restraint: Andy is not depressive, not dramatic, just deeply, historically tired.

This is the film's most conservative insight: immortality is not a gift. It is a burden. The ability to live without dying means watching everyone you love die while you continue. It means fighting the same wars under different names. It means discovering that human nature does not change, that the things you fight for in one century are undone in the next, and that you will be there to watch it happen again. The film takes this burden seriously in ways most superhero films cannot: because the characters have actually lived through centuries, their weariness is earned rather than performed.

The film's warrior ethic is its most traditionally compelling element. Andy, Joe, Nicky, and Booker operate as a military unit built on centuries of trust. Their combat effectiveness comes from absolute discipline, absolute loyalty, and absolute honesty with each other about their own failures. When Booker betrays the group, the punishment is exile: one hundred years of separation. The moral framework is warriors': loyalty is sacred, betrayal is the worst crime, and consequences are real. This is not a world where feelings are discussed in therapy. It is a world where actions determine belonging.

I want to address the Joe and Nicky element directly, because it is significant and the marketing obscured it. Joe (Marwan Kenzari) and Nicky (Luca Marinelli) are a gay couple who have been together for roughly nine hundred years. They met as soldiers on opposite sides of the Crusades, killed each other, were reborn side by side, and fell in love. The film treats their relationship with genuine seriousness. A scene where a mercenary mocks Joe by calling him 'his boyfriend' prompts an extended monologue from Joe about what Nicky is to him: 'He's more to me than you can dream.' The monologue is written and performed with real emotion.

For conservative viewers, this is where the film's woke element lands hardest. Joe and Nicky are not background characters. They are central. Their relationship is not ambiguous. The film presents their centuries-long bond as among the most authentic forms of love in the story.

Here is what makes this more complicated than a straight progressive box-check: the film's treatment of Joe and Nicky fits within the film's broader warrior ethic. Their love is presented as the deepest form of loyalty, the most durable bond. The film is not using them to make a political statement about gay rights; it is using them to illustrate what nine hundred years of shared sacrifice creates between two people. Whether that argument is persuasive to conservative viewers will depend on their specific objections to LGBTQ representation. The film is not camp, not performative, not using the relationship to score progressive points. It is using the relationship as a genuine expression of the film's theme: that what makes immortal existence bearable is the people you fight beside.

The villain (Merrick, played by Harry Melling) is a pharmaceutical executive who wants to exploit the immortals' regeneration for profit. The anti-Big Pharma framing is explicitly progressive and on-the-nose. Merrick is less a character than a target: young, entitled, willing to torture for profit, dismissive of human suffering. This is the film's weakest ideological element and its weakest narrative element simultaneously.

Chiwetel Ejiofor's Copley provides the film's most interesting moral complexity. He works with Merrick but is motivated by personal grief (his wife died of a disease he hoped the immortals' biology could cure). His arc, from collaborator to ally, is the film's most human journey.

KiKi Layne's Nile brings genuine emotion to what could have been a standard 'new recruit' role. Her disorientation at discovering her immortality, her grief at being permanently separated from her family, and her eventual integration into the team are handled with more psychological realism than the genre usually allows.

The action sequences are unusually strong for a Netflix production. Prince-Bythewood shoots combat with clarity and consequence: you always know where people are, what they are trying to do, and what it costs them. The pharmacy fight sequence is the film's action highlight, balancing choreography with character in ways that most superhero films sacrifice one for the other.

The Old Guard earns its TRADITIONAL LEAN verdict not by hiding its progressive elements but because its warrior ethics, its treatment of loyalty and betrayal, its meditation on the burden of outliving everyone you love, and its presentation of sacrifice as the condition of service all resonate with traditional values. The gay couple and the anti-pharma villain are real woke elements. But the film's bones are more traditional than its surface.
summary.oneLiner: Charlize Theron leads immortal warriors through a meditation on sacrifice and loyalty that is more traditional at its core than its progressive elements suggest.
summary.verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN. The film's warrior ethos, loyalty-over-everything moral framework, and treatment of immortality as burden rather than gift are genuinely traditional. The gay couple (Joe and Nicky) is the film's most significant progressive element and is present, central, and not backgrounded. The anti-Big Pharma villain is ideologically predictable. But the scores split: the traditional elements run deeper than the progressive ones in the film's actual dramatic weight.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults who enjoy action films and can navigate LGBTQ content that is present but not politically aggressive will find The Old Guard unexpectedly rewarding. The film takes its warrior ethic seriously. Betrayal has real consequences. Loyalty is treated as sacred. Immortality is presented as a burden that demands purpose. These are traditional values. Joe and Nicky's relationship is the line that many conservative viewers will draw, and it is a meaningful element of the film, not a detail you can skip past. Adults who can engage with the film despite that element will find an action film more interested in character and consequence than most. Adults who cannot will find it frustrating, because the relationship is not incidental.
summary.parentalGuidance: R. Best for ages 16 and up. The violence is graphic and frequent. The LGBTQ content (a gay male couple in a central role) is substantial and should factor into viewing decisions for families. No sexual content beyond a kiss. Thematic depth is appropriate for older teenagers and adults.

tropeAudit.name: Gay Couple as Central Heroic Characters
tropeAudit.description: Joe and Nicky are a gay couple who have been together for nine hundred years. Their relationship is central to the film's emotional architecture: their love is presented as the deepest form of loyalty the film depicts. A monologue where Joe describes what Nicky means to him is one of the film's most emotionally resonant moments. This is transferred directly from the source graphic novel. The relationship is presented as genuine and serious, not campy or performative.

tropeAudit.name: Female Warrior as Superior Physical and Strategic Leader
tropeAudit.description: Andy leads the team by virtue of age, experience, and combat skill. She is the unquestioned leader of a group that includes three men. Her authority is never challenged by gender. The film presents female physical and strategic dominance as unremarkable, which is progressive in framing but authentic to the premise: a woman who has been fighting for three thousand years would be the best warrior alive.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Corporate / Anti-Big Pharma Villain
tropeAudit.description: Merrick is a pharmaceutical executive who wants to exploit the immortals' regenerative biology for profit. He is willing to capture and torture them to extract value. The film frames corporate profit-seeking as the villain's entire motivation: Merrick is not evil in a complex way, but specifically in a capitalism-as-exploitation way. The anti-Big Pharma framing is explicit and politically predictable.

tropeAudit.name: Diverse International Ensemble (Race and Gender Mix)
tropeAudit.description: The immortal team spans races, ethnicities, and genders: a Scythian woman, a French soldier (Booker), a Crusade-era Maghrebi man (Joe), an Italian man (Nicky), and a contemporary Black American Marine (Nile). This diversity is plausible given the immortals' origins across different historical periods and cultures, but is also a conscious progressive casting choice.

tropeAudit.name: Moral Ambiguity of Extra-State Violence
tropeAudit.description: The team operates as mercenaries outside government authority. Their morality is self-defined: they choose missions they consider just, regardless of official mandates. The film presents this extra-institutional moral authority sympathetically. For conservatives who believe in institutional authority and rule of law, the framing of independent armed operators choosing their own moral targets is mildly progressive.

tropeAudit.name: Sacrifice and Duty to Protect Humanity
tropeAudit.description: The central question of the film is why the immortals continue to fight. Andy is losing her faith that their centuries of sacrifice have made any difference. The film's answer, provided through Copley's research, is that their actions have had ripple effects across history that they could not see: a life saved led to a breakthrough that saved millions. The moral framework is duty-based: you protect people not because you can see the outcome but because protection is the right thing to do. This is traditional warrior ethics.

tropeAudit.name: Brotherhood and Found Family Across Centuries
tropeAudit.description: The team's cohesion, built over decades and centuries, is the film's most emotionally compelling element. They know each other completely. They have fought through each other's deaths and rebirths. The bond is not friendship exactly; it is something more like the bond of shared suffering, shared purpose, and shared survival. When Booker betrays them, the punishment of exile is devastating precisely because this bond is sacred. Found family built through sacrifice and loyalty is a deeply traditional value.

tropeAudit.name: Loyalty and Honor Among Warriors
tropeAudit.description: The warrior code the team operates by is strict: you protect your people, you tell each other the truth, and betrayal has consequences. When Booker sells them out, the team does not forgive him immediately. They exile him for a century. The film treats this not as harshness but as justice: the code exists because trust is the only thing that makes their work possible. Warrior loyalty as sacred duty is a traditional value.

tropeAudit.name: Immortality as Burden, Not Gift
tropeAudit.description: The film consistently frames immortality as something to be endured, not celebrated. Andy's exhaustion is the film's emotional foundation. Nile's grief at being permanently separated from her family (who will age and die while she does not) is treated with genuine sorrow. The film does not romanticize the ability to live forever. This is consistent with traditional religious views: eternal life is not the goal; life lived well and ended meaningfully is. Immortality without death is presented as its own kind of prison.

tropeAudit.name: Mentorship Across Generations
tropeAudit.description: Andy's reluctant mentorship of Nile is the film's traditional mentorship arc. An ancient, experienced warrior teaches a new one not just combat technique but the psychological and moral dimensions of their shared existence. Andy does not want a new recruit; she eventually accepts responsibility for one. The passing of hard-won wisdom from experienced to inexperienced is a traditional mechanism for preserving culture and knowledge.

detailed_analysis.warrior_ethics: The Old Guard's traditional score comes primarily from its warrior ethics, which are more developed than most action films. The team's code involves absolute loyalty, honest assessment of failure, real consequences for betrayal, and duty-based motivation (protect people because that is what warriors do, not because you can guarantee a good outcome). These values are not progressive; they are ancient. The film is drawing on warrior traditions that predate modern political categories. This is why the traditional score competes effectively with the progressive elements.
detailed_analysis.immortality_as_theme: The film uses immortality not as a power fantasy but as a philosophical problem: what gives life meaning when it cannot end? The answer the film eventually arrives at is relational and purpose-based: the people you fight beside and the ripple effects of your actions across time. This is not a specifically progressive answer. It is a human one. Conservatives who believe in duty, service, and the importance of community will find more here than the progressive framing suggests.
detailed_analysis.netflix_success: The Old Guard became one of Netflix's most-watched original films at the time of its release (78 million households in 4 weeks). A sequel was greenlit and eventually released in 2024 (The Old Guard 2). The film's success demonstrated that action films with diverse casts and progressive elements can find massive audiences on streaming platforms.

comparison_films.title: John Wick
comparison_films.comparison: The obvious action comparison: a lone exceptional warrior with a specific combat style operating outside official structures. John Wick is more purely traditional (male protagonist, male-coded world, grief as motivation) and more purely entertainment-focused. The Old Guard is more interested in its characters' psychology and less in stylized violence for its own sake. Both films take their worlds seriously and reward viewers who pay attention to the world-building.

comparison_films.title: Highlander
comparison_films.comparison: The obvious premise comparison: immortal warriors across history, eventually limited in number. Highlander's immortals are competitive (there can be only one); The Old Guard's are cooperative. Both films deal with the psychological cost of outliving everyone you love. Highlander is more traditionally masculine in structure; The Old Guard is more emotionally expansive.

comparison_films.title: Black Widow
comparison_films.comparison: Another female-led action film with a found-family structure and a villain who exploits and controls women. Black Widow is more overtly feminist in its politics; The Old Guard's politics are more embedded in the action. Both received middling critical reviews relative to their budgets. The Old Guard has aged better in audience estimation.
